entry.title: 3 Nice Days
entry.content:
I went on a solo trip to the Côte d’Azur in the mid of May (arguably a very good time) and I thought it might be cool if I wrote about it. Before my ability to write and do art get any worse than they already are, here comes this travel + a little bit of art blog from my stay in Nice, FR. I have probably written a little too much about what was going through my head, but eh, might as well write more bs than prune it to make it more palatable (why take time doing something ai does well anyway). I have started giving much more time to my art too, and in this blog you will see some plein-air paintings and some that were made in the comfort of my dorm after the trip. I have also limited this blogpost to the city of Nice so that the length stays manageable (or so I thought).

Day 1 - May 12th

Had an early TGV to Paris. Took me some 1.5 hours to get there. I somehow had the time to take a printout of some random Inverse Reinforcement Learning slides before, so I started reading them while on train. I am the kind of person who just cannot sleep when I am travelling, so nothing like some performative ML paper/slides reading to amp up the cortisol. I reach Paris Gare de l’Est about little before 8am. Being a champ now at changing to the metro, I quickly check if any of my previously (expensively) bought navigo cards had any trips. And one of them did yayy. I side eye the metro line to be taken and the direction (lest someone identifies that this is a clueless tourist), I move through the turnstiles among the tens of Parisian salary people (huh imagine) and get into the M5 going towards Place d’Italie. GMaps had told me that the closest I can get to Gare du Lyon through this metro line, was through Bastille. And since I had not yet actually been there, I decided I might as well get out at Bastille, look at it, and then walk my way to Gare du Lyon. I had enough time, weather seemed nice and it was early in the morning. So I do exactly that. There were fences around the Bastille monument, but it was tall enough and I took a few pictures. Quickly side eyed (we do this a lot) the way to the next Gare and found that we can walk along the Seine. As I am walking along the Seine, I see about 50 camps along the sidewalk. It was kind of weird and when I travel and I see things like this, I always get reflective about life, infrastructure and the concept of home.

I take my time getting into the main street at the end of which is my destination. I do want a croissant now. I stop at La Parisienne, get myself 2 croissants (one of my classics when I want something on the go) and keep walking towards the Gare. Since it’s early in the morning, I give myself the liberty to enjoy the Parisian Haussmann buildings, trees, people and signboards. Of course. I get into the Gare and it is extremely important that as soon as you enter a train station, you keep your phone inside and look up. At the massive screens that have all the trains. First, if you want, look at your train and verify if it even exists. Then look at all the potential places trains from here can take you to. We do some scanning around, look at the red hat children’s troop possibly going on a very fun trip, the one kid who is crying, two adults consoling him and a passerby drunkard saying something to the kid, maybe as a consolation too. Let’s check if we have enough water, if not then we will be onto a side-quest to find a water fountain somewhere. We do have enough water never mind. Time to eat the croissants now. I find my place on a singular cube facing an elevator, between a group of 70 year old francophones, who are tying their suitcases with the free identification tags and saying my bonjours and nods, I sit down. I eat my croissants and oh so lovely. I didnt have to wait long because my next train to Nice is already at the platform. So I make my way there, get my ticket scanned, find my place and sit there. I find that it is the last seat in the coach but hey it has a window. The train starts around 9am and wooo we are on our way to Sud de France.

In the first three hours we have already reached Marseille. The British women in front of me - “I think we are in Lyon. My grandmother’s town was near Lyon and Dijon. Looks like a big city, might be Lyon.” Ma’am we literally saw the sea 5 minutes ago. But anyway that’s okay. Also, not that anyone cares, but the person next to me watched two films in 5 hours, had another handwritten list of films that were official selections at Cannes. So yeah he was going to Cannes. After Marseille, we keep stopping at some of the South of France hotspots - St. Tropez, Toulon, Cannes, Antibes and finally Nice. My hostel is right across the train station, so I check-in in almost no time. I stay at Hotel Antares (if anyone needs this information) and I would rate the hostel experience a 4/5. A modest breakfast is included, lockers exist but outside the room, bathroom was pretty nice.

It is probably around 4pm now, the sunset is not going to be for another 5 hours and so I quickly put on a summer outfit and head out. I walk towards the beach, which is a 20 minutes away but the walk is nice. I cross the Fountaine du Soleil at Place Massena and I am greeted with the amazingly blue Mediterranean through the Quai des Etats-Unis. I had been very excited to go to the beach since I had planned the trip and it looked absolutely worth it. I walked along the sea towards the Castel side. Checked my saved pins to check if we can cover any of the spots we planned to see. An ice-cream from Fenocchio sounded very nice. I crossed the road, very close to the Cours Saleya market and admired the town. The architecture around was so beautiful, all with the pretty pastel colours and the blue sky.

Walked through vielle ville to Place Rossetti and got myself a Tartuffe from Fenocchio. I got one with Gianduja (chocolate mixed with hazelnut paste) and Cookies parfums (flavours), and they add Chantilly on it along with grilled pralines and hot chocolate. It was made by one of the senior guys at the shop because maybe it’s not ordered that often? Anyway, as someone who rarely goes beyond the chocolate flavours, I loved it and give it a 5/5. The Cathedrale Saint-Reparate de Nice is very pretty too. I then walked around the streets of the old town, and this is one of those times when I absolutely try not to check the maps. It is a lovely time to explore around and when you are in a such a pretty scenic part of town, it is probably better if I get lost anyway.

At some point though, I did meet the sea once again and took my time walking along it and admiring the town. As I kept walking towards and beyond the Colline du Chateau, I realised I had found the port. There were the rich-people yachts parked into the port and as the sun was setting down, the other side of the port was glowing yellow orange. I postponed going across the port to another day, and took a left towards Place Garibaldi. Mind you, I didn’t even know what it was and if it was worth visiting. You just bump into interesting spots when you allow yourself to saunter around. Fuck around. Find out. I sat down there under the shade of some big tree along with fellow resters and managed to check my phone at this point to decide my next quest. Since I had only had the Tartuffe for whatever meal that was, I decided to try another one of the popular nicoise food items - Socca. Actually now that I think about it, I hadn’t decided it then and there, but when I had already started walking in some random direction and saw a traditional looking shop selling Socca. Socca is essentially a thicker crepe made of chickpea flour, olive oil and salt. Very close to an indian cheela but very filling. I was still munching on it till the end of the day and it certainly kept the hunger away. Most tourists usually get it at the Cours Saleya market and I can totally see it as a banger street food to keep you fulfilled while shopping for fresh flowers and produce.

As the evening had started setting in now and with my newfound Socca-fuelled energy, I decided to climb the Colline du Chateau and had planned to sit there through the sunset. It was barely a few stairs but the view was still immaculate. I could see the chemically different blue colours of the sea, there was a street guitarist playing some tunes, some lovers sitting at the edge admiring the view and other lovers judging the daredevils together. I took the middle route and sat on one of fences falling through which might not have killed me except for a few scratches (that would have been great for plot). And as soon as I sat and had finished peeling my orange, a lady officer joined us, specifically looked at me to say c’est ferme. At 8pm. Ehh the sunset was still like 1.5 hours away but well I had to climb back down now. Was definitely staying for the sunset by the beach so I just took a seat near the #ILoveNice and chilled while the golden hour led up to the dusk. At some point, after being awake since 4:45am, it was sleepy time and be ready for my adventures next day.

Day 2 - May 13th

The day starts a little late (by my desi standards) but I still am able to catch the hostel’s cereal and coffee breakfast. I didn’t have much plans starting out today. I knew the weather might be nice generally so I was supposed to be outdoors all day.

I don’t exactly remember what I planned to do but I started walking anyway. (story of my life)

I walked through the Place Massena once again, took a left towards the potential nicer areas. Wait, I remember, I wanted to go to the sandy beaches of Villefranche-sur-Mer. And so I start walking in that general direction. I had hoped that at some point, I will hop onto a bus and that will take me there but, as it often happens, I found myself on an accidental hike. Through some corniche, I was already gaining elevation - there were stairs ahead of me, but hey there were pretty orange rooftops and the Alps behind me. At multiple points I felt like I was borderline trespassing and could easily look into people’s backyards and kitchens. I felt very free though (as actual trespassers usually do). Climbing a bunch of stairs, crossing a few main roads, I reached somewhere close to the Fort du Mont Alban. We don’t go there but we are in the right direction.

The great thing about an accidental elevation gain is that eventually you will have the joy of some fun elevation loss. And I found that joy not long after when I saw a board saying “Commune de Villefrance s/ Mer”. I could see the sea and I knew that was where I needed to be, so I climbed down by any observable set of stairs. Again borderline trespassing. I spent an abnormally long time at one of the longer staircases because it seemed like a nice spot to take some pictures. Eventually, I was in the main part of the town. How do I know that? I passed through a big church. It was the Église Saint-Michel de Villefranche-sur-Mer but I did not go in. I had gotten two croissants at a local boulangerie and was happily waddling down whatever stairs might take me to the beach. The town itself was extremely pretty, pastel and quaint. Now, I meet the sea once again. I make my way to the Plage des Marinieres, which isn’t as rocky as the main Nice beach. And so less painful for a quick dip. I played with the sea a bit, sat on a rock and painted.

Around 2pm, I planned my way back to Nice for some quick lunch and the 3pm biking tour I had booked before. The train that would take me to Nice Riquier in 2 minutes was right above this beach so it was a very short walk up some stairs. From the Nice Riquier station, I make my way to the Port Lympia and sit for a very quick lunch at FOAM. I order for an aperol spritz and a pizzette. The pizzette was fresh and very well-seasoned, the spritz was just spritz ig. I got a little late as I speed-walked to the start point of my bike tour but at least I wasn’t going to be hungry.

My 3 hour bike tour started from Cours Saleya and our first stop was Place Garibaldi. Italy and France both have had major roles in the history of Nice, and this spot has architecture and vibe inspired from the Italian side. From here we climb up the Colline du Chateau and get to very pretty view points both of the port as well as the old city. There is a waterfall here, because apparently at some point there was water shortage here, so we checked that out. The waterfall also made a tiny little rainbow among the rocks which was cute. What was also cute was a man getting his picture taken with his hat a little over his head as a photographic effect of water falling through his hat into his head (probably?). From here we bike down (the joy of descent is 10x when biking btw), ride along the beach through the Quai des Etats-Unis to the Promenade des Anglais, looking at the famous blue chairs of Nice and eventually stopping at Le Negresco, the very very luxury hotel that was made one year before the first world war. From here we bike along the lanes of the not-so-old part of the city and reach Russia. Cathedrale Saint Nicholas de Nice, is a Russian Orthodox Church whose premises are under the Russian jurisdiction, and not the French. It is a very attractive church and they also have bunnies :).

From here, we now reach the best viewpoint in Nice (according to Alfred, our bike guide) - and this took me back to Fort du Mont Alban. The ascent was a little tough at this point but the descent through the beautiful forest area with the cool cool air, made up for it easily.

After the tour was done, my calf muscles were already pressing their SOS buttons so I decided to get a simple focaccia sandwich from Foca to eat and sit at the beach as the sun set.

Day 3 - May 15th

May 14th was my extremely ambitious and exerting trip to Cannes, Antibes and Monaco. We will cover them at some later date. I spent the 15th in Nice and I did have some plans for today.

Given that I had some physically strenuous past few days, I decided today was going to be a more flowy-dress tote-bag kinda day. I start from the famous flowers and produce market of Cours Saleya, get myself a box of fresh pineapples and melons and also four crispy madeleines from Mellow Madeleine. I do some shopping at Trésors Publics, which I randomly went into but it a was very cool shop with all items made in France.

From here, we make our way to the Matisse Museum. It was either a 40 min walk or a 10 min bus ride, and in the most un-geetika move ever, I take the bus. The museum itself is a little out of the central town because Matisse used to stay nearby in his Nice era. I hope none of the Matisse’s fans read this, but honestly I did not much appreciate his work. Fauvism is probably a little too interesting for my plain vanilla brain. The museum shop was also … mid.

It is around 2:30pm now and I was very hungry with no hopes of getting anything good easily. I make my way to the food kiosk next to the museum, and somehow order for a local plate of Farcis Nicoise. I don’t question what it is but it looked like a stuffed vegetable type dish we sometimes make in India, and honestly, this was one of the few times I liked a french dish. The staff at the kiosk were also very sweet, and I could sense a nice vibe around me. Two uncles playing chess, a group of middle aged women having a blast and 4-5 different groups of adults playing pétanque in the park. Life was good (atleast for these people in a first world country). After this, I catch a bus back into town, get myself a delicious la fameuse focaccia from Babel Babel and then some more beach-relaxation with a Fenocchio ice-cream time happens.

Few more bonus hours on 16th May

Today was a Saturday and my train to Marseille was at 10:50am. I had some time in the morning to potentially cover one more spot and this became the Saturday Marche des Antiquities (antiquities market), at the Place de Palais de Justice. There were thousands of ancient postcards, posters and antique cutlery items. I spent an abnormal amount of time checking every 1890s-1900s Le Monde newspaper to see if any of the dates were interesting for me to take back. I spent even more abnormal amount of time reading through the old postcards because I love reading what people before us used to write to their loved ones while travelling. I love to experience these random snapshots of some Jacqueline’s and Marie-Lou’s from the 1990s, and humans are sometimes so cute ehehe.

Okay so that’s a wrap girls and boys. Hope you had fun, if not then you shouldn’t have read this far man, find something else to do.

As I mentioned before, this blog intentionally skips my side quests to some other parts of the French Riviera, and ideally they could get a blog of their collective own. Who knows. I am also a little tired of writing at this point, but aha I still have to work on my manuscript. So more writing here I come.

PS: Tools I used for my art: the Moleskine Sketch Album, Winsor & Newton watercolours, Sakura Pigma Sensei 0.4mm, Faber-Castell Pitt Artist Pen fine liners and my sheer will to make bad art.
entry.summary: World can only watch as I turn a beach vacation into a hardcore-25k-steps/day-borderline-dehydrated expedition

entry.title: A gentle introduction to RL Theory

link.title: A gentle introduction to RL Theory

entry.content:
If only I had written this blog 6 months back, I could have moved on to write and blog about much more interesting stuff. But anyway, here we are - A gentle (hopefully intuitive) introduction to RL. Before we start, check out this primer on language and notation at the end of the doc - the best way to tackle difficult math, I have found, is to know how to speak math as it is written. This gets easier with time, but I’ll try to keep this primer resourceful at least for our purposes currently. I have tried to also add alt text over the formulas, so you can verify their verbalisation.

In this blog, I’d want to cover an intuitive understanding of RL and some of its bedrock ideas around environment, reward, state, Markov Processes, policy and value functions. A majority of the content is inspired and taken from 3 main sources - my notes from UCL and David Silver’s RL course, IITM and B. Ravindran’s RL course and the amazing Sutton and Barto Reinforcement Learning - An Introduction.

First Dip

Machine Learning is a paradigm under AI where given some historical data and expected outputs, a model is learned that could potentially derive outputs with new unseen data. It is nice because we have so much data that finding patterns and deriving a function through automation is fundamentally easier than ever. There are three kinds of machine learning methodologies, based on the existence of feedback or its timing along the training.

Supervised Learning - data and feedback are both instantly available.

Unsupervised Learning - data is available but feedback doesn’t exist.

Reinforcement Learning - data appears but the feedback is delayed.

Given ample literature on supervised and unsupervised learning and their applications, I’d jump straight to where we use RL.

RL is the study of sequential decision-making under uncertainty.

Here,

sequential - a paradigm that changes and modifies with time and interaction → much like the real world. I am not a ubiquitous narrator, but I (RL agent) actively participate in how I respond to the environment variables and how those variables change with my responses.

decision-making - I have the “agency” to choose a response (/action)

uncertainty - I don’t know what responses lead to what changes, initially and how good or bad they are because my feedback is delayed.

The basic RL Framework

Terminology

  • History: the sequence of observations, actions and rewards over the past. The history at time t denotes all the observable variables up to a time t. The future is dependent on this history.

\(H_t = A_1, O_1, R_1, A_2, …, A_t, O_t, R_t\)

  • State: Summary of all the required information to determine what happens next. The state is a function of the history.

\(S_t = f(H_t)\)

  • Environment State and Agent State:

    Environment State is the environment’s private representation - all the information that environment uses to pick the next observation/reward.

    Agent State is the agent’s internal representation - all the information the agent uses to pick the next action. And this is precisely all the information used by RL algorithms.

\(Environment State : S_t^e, Agent State : S_t^a\)

Components of an RL Agent

An RL agent may include one or more of these functional information -

  • Policy function describes the agent’s behaviour

    • It is a map from state to action
    • A deterministic policy would mean that a unique action ensures the best reward whenever state S happens. A stochastic policy, on the other hand, does not guarantee this, and an action does not have a unique link to the state.

  • Value function describes the utility or goodness of each state and/or action

    • The value function is a prediction of the future reward given the information state and available action choices. We want to choose the action that maximises the value function.

  • Model function describes the agent’s representation of the environment.

    • A model predicts what the environment will do in response to a state and an action over that state.

The majority of all RL algorithms are designed for optimising over these three components and making the agent better at maximising rewards.

The Markov Property

“The future is independent of the past given the present.”

This means that the state St is a sufficient statistic of the future. All of the history of observations, actions and rewards can be explained and encompassed through this one variable, and is sufficient to predict the next action and observation.

Markov Process: is a memoryless random process, i.e. a sequence of random states S1,S2,… with the Markov property. A Markov process (or Markov chain) is a tuple <S,P> where:

  • S is a finite set of states

  • P is a state-transition probability matrix

    • For a Markov state S and successor state S’, the state transition probability (PSS’)is the probability that given I am in state S and by taking some action, I go next to state S’. A state transition matrix P then defines these transition probabilities from all states S to all successor states S’.

\(P_{SS’} = P[S_{t+1} = s’|S_t=s]\)

Why discount? To keep the math bounded and avoid infinite returns in cyclic markov chains. It is also more likely (wrt rich environments) that immediate rewards have more value in determining utility of an action than a delayed reward that’s harder to map. It is still possible to use discounted Markov reward processes if all sequences definitely terminate.

In the (hopefully soon) blogpost, I’d go deeper into the math of value functions, returns, the Bellman Equations and introduce the paradigm of dynamic programming in RL.

entry.title: What I have been working on / summer of ‘24

link.title: What I have been working on / summer of ‘24

entry.content:
I have been very tardy in writing a third post haha. Bear with me though, I have a good enough reason. I find myself currently in a cafe drinking some mango sherbet. Its 33 degrees celsius in one of those towns where it dips to -40 in winters and you can see northern lights at the right place and time. They say its climate change. It crossed 53 degrees in Delhi too. That’s climate change too. I saw a post yesterday that said scientists already invented a glass type material that can be used to make buildings and generate energy simultaneously. And a comment below that was - “great wow, can’t wait to never hear about it ever again”. The way I chuckled and realised that that’s so true. Like imagine funding research for renewable sources of energy and still AL-ing oil, petroleum and coal companies. Why is it so difficult agh?

Unfortunately for me, environment is not something I have been actively thinking or working on. I have been in Canada for 2 months now. I have 1 month more. I am interning at a university here. The research has been around ultrasound as point-of-care to when a person walks into hospital emergency with a broken shoulder.

Canadian healthcare is free. This unfortunately also means that it is prone to a lot of delays. Let’s assume we all have a common friend Mike who has suffered trauma on his shoulder. He cannot move it, its paniful and he really misses swimming. He takes a consultation, doctor suspects that Mike has a rotator cuff tear and prescribes him to get an MRI scan. Rotator cuff tear means a torn shoulder tendon and MRI is medical gold standard to diagnose these tears. Mike takes an appointment for scan but he is scheduled for 10 weeks from now. Almost 2.5 months. To live with such a pain all this time is definitely not ideal.

MRI infrastructure is costly, resource-intensive, not accessible to everyone and hence prone to very long wait times. What if we use a simpler and dumber imaging paradigm then? My research proposes ultrasound imaging using a handheld probe that comes with its own tablet. This is portable, accessible and can even be used by lightly trained sonographers.

So at this point, we make Mike get his ultrasound “sweep” done. This sweep is like a long video of about 200-300 frames where each frame shows an ultrasound image at a specific angle of Mike’s shoulder. Ultrasound though has some problems itself. Although it is almost instant, it has a lot of noise. Most of these 200-300 frames are irrelevant and carry no important information about presence of tear or not. We want to be able to reduce this long long video to contain only the most diagnostically important few frames. For this, I have been working on a Deep Reinforcement Learning algorithm that picks the key frames/summary like a human radiologist would have.

The RL agent takes a decision at every frame to choose which frames will be included in the summary. If it makes a good decision and a good representative summary is created, the agent is rewarded. This way it learns what is expected of it. But if it makes a bad summary, it is penalised. This reward and penalty is a function of the next step of our pipeline - the deep learning classifer. This classifier is tasked to predict the presence of tear in Mike’s shoulder scan. Its confidence on its own prediction is key to judge how well the RL+classifier work.

Eventually when the classifier is fairly confident about its prediction, a report pops up on the sonographer’s tablet. This could be something like - ‘Our model is 94% confident that patient has a rotator-cuff tear’ (or something more professional). This is then communicated to Mike and his doctor. The doctor then can start targeted treatmet that came from this preliminary diagnosis and hopefully Mike then would be swimming way before his MRI appointment.

Do not judge the story and lack of all technical jargon. This had been my 3 minute thesis presentation infront people from various different backgrounds and I consider it a good low-level introduction to what I have been working on. I could use jargon but I’ll be doing that a little later.

Besides this sweet deal, I have been attending some amazing sessions on Continual Learning and similar stuff. My first week here was attending this very cool conference called Upper Bound. Couldnt have had a better introduction to academia here than that. Debating about RL in a room full of the best RL researchers. Rich Sutton, Doina Precup, Csaba Szepesvari, Martha and Adam White, Marlos Machado - all amazing. I also networked a bit here and there, got to know about the culture here and traveled through mountains and badlands and lakes and farmers’ markets. All have made it a nice experience. I wouldn’t lie, I dont think this could have been my best attempt at documenting my experience here. Maybe when I can, I’ll write up another one. But till then, this goes up and stays.

PS - And in case you worry why the subtitle contains “hospitals”, the nearest train station to me is the Health sciences station and I have to cross the hospital from end to end internally to get there. So I was in hospitals more often than a normal person would. Plus, a labmate who did ultrasound scans took us to a cast clinic to show how he does the scan, and where our application eventually works. So that’s about it. I have been pretty healthy don’t worry.
entry.summary: conferences, hospitals, ethernets and libraries / heat warnings and snow falls

entry.title: The divide-and-conquer of patriarchy and why it’s harmful to humanity

link.title: The divide-and-conquer of patriarchy and why it’s harmful to humanity

entry.content:
There is a significant issue with feminism and how people view it off late. I just read this particular excerpt from The Second Sex by Simone de Beauvoir - “The woman herself believes that her personal life does not dispense her from the duties she assumed in marrying; she does not want her husband to be deprived of the advantages he would have had in marrying a ‘real woman’; she wants to be elegant, a good housekeeper and a devoted mother as wives traditionally are.”

It is interesting how a lot of the debate around feminism these days is about the division occurring between angry feminists who hate men and consciously or subconsciously look down upon the feminists who want to inherently be dainty, good housewives and serve their families like in the status quo. This gives us two definitions of feminism. The latter group claims it to be simply the freedom of opportunity to be as they please and do as they please without societal restrictions to dictate what they wear/where they work. The former group, though, which originated before and is slowly being labelled as pseudo-feminism (I am not proclaiming if it should be or not yet), designs feminism as the philosophy of rigorous and consistent banishing of patriarchal structures around us. This includes countering and analysing every act/method by way of how it has historically kept women inferior and how men have easily risen away as superiors. And we let them.

Patriarchy has identified this rift and is using it against the whole idea of equality. They have historically favoured and glorified the superwomen and the women who happily submit to their fathers or husbands. SDB says, “The advantage man enjoys and which manifests itself from childhood onwards is that his vocation as a human being in no way contradicts his destiny as a male. […] He is not divided (between his roles as a human being and a bearer of masculinity). However, for a woman to accomplish her femininity (defined by men and most probably capitalists, but that’s a discussion for another day), she is required to be object and prey; that is, she must renounce her claims as a sovereign subject.” The destiny of a female is mostly always in conflict with her personality as an individual with intellect and passion. Conformity to custom is easier for men, while for women, it comes at the cost of losing their individuality. It’s a man’s world, after all; who is she kidding?

Coming back to our problem on how anti-feminists have conveniently divided feminists stems from the idea of freedom of opportunity and how opportunity in itself is biased behind centuries of gender indoctrination. Opportunity is only so ever bounded by what the system wants us to desire ourselves. Years of propaganda have shown women that they SHOULD want to give their family a clean abode, their husband a nourishing lunch and their children 20 hours of their day. A woman ought to prefer looking delicate and perfect (lest the neighbours talk about her hysteria or men want her less). Any less, and she is a careless woman. When she cannot choose herself over what society wants of her, she decides to pick the worst combination of both. She claims she chooses to live as a subordinate by her own will. It is her own will no doubt, but that will has roots in the society’s mutilation of women who choose to be contrarian.

What this needs, and I want to interpret the initial feminist struggle, was, too, a collective systemic shift in how women perceive their choices. A girl is more likely to believe in her freedom of opportunity when she knows nobody can question her sanity by digging out an example of another woman who “managed” everything well or who played with her hobbies whilst polishing the shoes of the good woman idea. It is important for our gender to collectively take ourselves more seriously than the “superwoman” society wants us to be. I may not want to use something as strong as “fight against”, but it is imperative, at this point, for us women to come together as a lot and redefine what femininity means. Don’t let the powerful people with useless things to make, money to monger, temples to follow and a conservative society to impress decide what femininity is for you. It is going to be a little tough for the women who define and know themselves first, but a few centuries were enough for patriarchy; let’s claim our place as human beings here.

In rage but optimism,

Geetika
entry.summary: Don’t let the powerful people with useless things to make, money to monger, temples to follow and a conservative society to impress decide what femininity is for you

entry.title: An introduction of the writer to the reader, if you will

link.title: An introduction of the writer to the reader, if you will

entry.content:
My head faces a dilemma presently. A part of me wants me to do well in my work or research without an explicit announcement on the internet about my arrival. The other understands the power of putting-myself-out-there and conversing about my interests, ideas, and analyses. This dilemma has been there for a while, but initially, it started out with a sense of under-fulfilment to the image of a confident technical writer. Now I think I want to write.

I want to write for the sake of anything I read or watch that takes me a while to catch or comprehend deeply. That wants me to prove if I get it after all. So here comes an attempt that hopefully takes my side.

I am Geetika, and as of April 2024 - I am a penultimate undergraduate pursuing a major in Computer Science Engineering and specialising in Artificial Intelligence. I wouldn’t exactly say that I wanted to be an engineer all my life, or I was coding and making chips since third grade because I hadn’t been that certain till pretty recently.

In my first semester of college, taking a course on Intelligent Systems (very introductory), I realised computer science is pretty cool. I started holding the idea that, at the end of the day, humans just want to create something as complex as them. I started loving CS. There began my exploration of Artificial Intelligence. It took me from Natural Language Processing to Game Theory to Computer Vision to Reinforcement Learning. I never found much passion for CS in my part of town, so it always seems like a contrarian way of dealing with the subject. But then I gradually understood that that’s the slower, more sensible way of knowing something. I am so glad I understood that by the end of the second year.

I started reading amazing research papers, following amazing researchers, and reading about their journeys through CS, and I am always very inspired. I am also an avid reader. Agatha Christie kindled the habit that has taken me from Stephen King to Brian Christian to Vaclav Smil. As Mark Twain said, “The man who does not read has no advantage over the man who cannot read.” This helps pretty well. I sketch+paint a few times a month to justify the overloaded art supplies drawer somehow.

Through these blogs, I’d want to document what I have learned, explore the craft, and chronicle how I break and fix stuff. This is definitely more of a personal journal than something I need readers for. Feel free to accompany though; I’d love to hear from you.

With admiration and gratitude,

Geetika
